Wrong

You were within your rights to cut the branches back to the boundary line. In most common-law jurisdictions, a tree owner has no right to let branches or roots encroach on a neighbour's land, and the neighbour may cut them back to the boundary without the owner's permission. However, you did two things that went beyond that right.

First, you cut "exactly to the boundary" from your side. That phrasing suggests you may have trimmed right up to the trunk or into the part of the tree that belongs to your neighbour, rather than stopping at the line where the branches cross it. The lawful limit is usually the boundary line itself; anything beyond that is your neighbour's property.

Second, you left the cut branches on her side. In many places, the branches (and any fruit on them) remain the tree owner's property once cut. Leaving them there can look like you're claiming them or dumping your work on her, and it's a common source of dispute. The usual practice is to offer them back to the owner, or at least make sure she knows they're there and can collect them.

The bigger issue is the tone of the dispute. You acted on a clear legal right, but you did it without telling her. From her perspective, someone went into her garden and altered her tree without asking. Even if the act was lawful, the lack of communication is what made her furious. A quick call or note saying "I'm trimming the branches that overhang my bed; I'll leave the cuttings for you" would have prevented most of the anger.

So: the trimming itself was largely justified, but doing it without notice and leaving the cuttings on her side were the mistakes. If you want to keep the peace, apologise for not telling her, offer the cuttings (or ask what she wants done with them), and let her know you'll check with her next time. If the tree is healthy and the shade is the main problem, you might also consider shade-tolerant vegetables or a light-reflecting mulch to help your bed, which can reduce the need for further cutting.
